Patrick Hamilton
păt´rĭk hăm´ĭl-ton
n. (Patrick Hamilton, 1504–1528, first preacher and martyr of the Scottish Reformation, burned at St Andrews at the age of twenty-four)
Scottish personal name. His short Latin theses on law and gospel, translated by John Frith, are known as Patrick's Places.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Patrick Hamilton was of royal blood, titular abbot of Fearn, and a student at Paris and Louvain when Luther's writings were first being read. Returning to St Andrews he preached justification by faith, fled to Germany when the archbishop moved against him, studied at the new Protestant university of Marburg, and there wrote his Places, a set of propositions distinguishing the law, which shows sin, from the gospel, which shows Christ. Their burden is Paul's: “by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin” (Rom 3:20), and “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28). He went back to Scotland knowing what it would cost. Invited to a conference at St Andrews, he was condemned and burned before St Salvator's College on 29 February 1528; the fire was badly made and he suffered for some six hours. His last words, like Stephen's, were “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Act 7:59). A contemporary remarked to the archbishop that if he burned any more he should burn them in cellars, for the smoke of Master Patrick Hamilton had infected as many as it blew upon.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines martyr as one who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel; and, in a general sense, one who suffers death in defence of any cause.

MARTYR, n. One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel.

2. One who suffers death in defence of any cause.

Key Scripture

Rom 3:20 — "Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin."

Rom 3:28 — "Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law."

Gal 2:16 — "Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified."

Act 7:59 — "And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."

Modern Corruption

Hamilton died for the distinction between law and gospel, which the modern church has largely dissolved into a single message of moral improvement with Christ as helper.

expand to see more

The Places turn on a simple contrast: the law says, Pay what thou owest; the gospel says, Christ hath paid it. Much modern preaching collapses the two, preaching the gospel as a programme of life change and the law as good advice, so that hearers never despair of themselves and never rest in Christ. That is the medieval confusion Hamilton came home to oppose, and it has returned in evangelical dress.

The recovery is to preach the law in its full severity, to shut every mouth, and the gospel in its full freeness, to open every hand. A young man burned for six hours at St Andrews because he would not blur that line; the smoke of it carried the Reformation through Scotland.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify; ergon (G2041), work, deed; epignosis (G1922), knowledge.

expand to see more

Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous; Romans 3:20, 28, Galatians 2:16.

Greek ergon (G2041) — work, deed; Romans 3:28, Galatians 2:16.

Greek epignosis (G1922) — full knowledge, recognition; Romans 3:20.

Usage

"“by the law is the knowledge of sin” (Rom 3:20) — the first half of Patrick's Places."

"“a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28) — the second half."

"“Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Act 7:59) — his words at the stake."
